title: Twelve days that wet the rice bowl
subtitle: NISAR S-band radar sees the Cauvery delta through the first northeast-monsoon storms, 6 → 18 October 2026

flags.label: Likely radio-frequency interference
flags.note: A diffuse oval HV glow with no field structure. It sits in a different place on each date (it moved), and ISRO's release notes warn of residual RFI in this product baseline. Analyst flag after visual review: treat as an artifact, not land change.

chapters.title: India's rice bowl, under cloud
body: The Cauvery delta (Thanjavur, Thiruvarur, Nagapattinam, Mayiladuthurai, Karaikal) grows a large share of Tamil Nadu's rice. October is when the short kuruvai crop is harvested and the long samba crop goes in, just as the northeast monsoon arrives.

Monsoon cloud hides the delta from optical satellites for weeks at a time. NISAR's S-band radar brings its own illumination and passes straight through the cloud, so it imaged the whole delta on both dates.

chapters.title: What the radar colours mean
body: Red is HH, the same-polarisation echo: bright for rough ground and for buildings, where walls and ground form corner reflectors. Green is HV, the cross-polarised echo, created when the wave bounces around inside vegetation canopies. Blue is the HH/HV ratio.
Smooth water mirrors the radar away from the satellite and appears black: the Kollidam river, the coast and the Vedaranyam swamp. Towns glow pink-white. Crop and tree cover shows green.

chapters.title: Where the delta went dark
body: The change composite shows Date A in red and Date B in cyan. Red therefore marks surfaces that got darker by 18 October; cyan marks surfaces that got brighter.

Field after field in the central and eastern delta turned darker after 52–100 mm of rain fell between the passes (Thiruvarur 99.6 mm, Karaikal 88.8 mm, Nagapattinam 80.9 mm). The darkening follows field boundaries, not storm cells.
chapters.hypothesis: Standing water in paddy fields: rain ponding, or fields flooded and puddled for samba transplanting. Calm water reflects the radar away, which is why HH falls.
chapters.caveat: Not proven by radar alone. Flooded fields, wet bare soil and a change in crop stage can all lower HH. An optical image from a clear day, or a field visit, would confirm it.

chapters.title: Vedaranyam swamp fills up
body: The largest coherent darkening is in the Great Vedaranyam Swamp, behind the Point Calimere coast: 55 regions totalling about 1,717 ha, with HH falling about 6 dB (four times weaker) while HV barely moves.
chapters.hypothesis: Rain and runoff spreading a thin, smooth sheet of water across the mudflats and salt pans. That is the HH-dominant darkening that open water produces.
chapters.caveat: Tide level and wind at the two acquisition times also change how water and wet mud scatter. Both dates were acquired at 00:15 UTC (05:45 local), but the tide state is not known.

chapters.title: Where it got brighter
body: Across the drier western uplands, HH brightened slightly but almost everywhere: the delta-wide median ΔHH is about +1 dB.
chapters.hypothesis: Wetter soil. Water raises the soil's dielectric constant, so damp ground reflects more radar energy back to the satellite even when nothing visible has changed.
chapters.caveat: A small calibration offset between passes can also shift the whole scene. The robust z-score measures change relative to this background, so the shift does not create candidates by itself.

chapters.title: Not every change is real
body: The biggest statistical change in the delta, 3,095 ha near Thanjavur, is not land change. It is a soft, oval HV glow with no field pattern. On 6 October a similar glow sat farther south; by 18 October it had moved.

TerraTrace flags all 31 regions inside these glows (about 3,762 ha) as likely radio-frequency interference, and the totals here exclude them. A change map that cannot tell you what to distrust is not evidence.

chapters.title: From radar echoes to decisions
body: Twelve days, two radar passes and no clear sky were enough to map where water collected across about 10,500 km² of farmland, and to say how sure we are about each patch.

With NISAR's 12-day repeat this becomes a monitor: agriculture officers tracking samba transplanting, disaster teams watching monsoon waterlogging, wetland managers following the swamp. Every number traces back to the exact scene IDs and the processing steps.
